title: Denis Villeneuve Chose to Direct New James Bond Movie After ‘Dune 3’ Because ‘I Need a Powerful Rocket to Pull Me Away From Arrakis’
description: Denis Villeneuve recently told Empire that he returned to “Dune” for a third and final chapter so he can be “severe with the material,” and that hi
body:
Denis Villeneuve recently told Empire that he returned to “Dune” for a third and final chapter so he can be “severe with the material,” and that his upcoming James Bond movie will be the “very powerful rocket” he needs to “pull me away from Arrakis.” 

	“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite — I’m tired of it.’ I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he explained. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”
	

	Villeneuve, director of “Prisoners,” “Sicario” and “Arrival,” has not helmed a film outside the “Dune” franchise since “Part One” was released in 2021. “Dune: Part Two” hit theaters in 2024, and “Dune: Part Three” will debut on Dec. 18, 2026. 


	In June 2025, it was revealed that Villeneuve, a self-described “die-hard Bond fan,” will direct the next 007 movie. There’s been much speculation about who will take up the mantle after Daniel Craig’s 15-year run. Gary Oldman recently claimed that the next James Bond has already been picked, but no official casting announcement has been made. 

	Based on Frank Herbert’s “Dune Messiah,” “Dune: Part Three” chronicles Paul Atreides’ fall from prophetic liberator to tyrannical emperor. Timothée Chalamet stars as Paul alongside Zendaya, Jason Momoa, Florence Pugh, Robert Pattinson, Anya Taylor-Joy, Rebecca Ferguson, Josh Brolin and Javier Bardem. 
	

	In her own sit-down with Empire, Zendaya discussed the arc of her character, Chani, in “Dune: Part 3.” She revealed that in the new film, Chani feels “a deep pain” and “a deep betrayal” as Paul becomes unrecognizable from the man she fell in love with. 

	“In the previous film, she opened herself up to the idea of letting someone in, allowing a space for love or gentleness,” she said. “Well, we see how that goes. That part of her life is not as present anymore.”

title: Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan Compete on Game Shows Hosted by David Byrne in the Retro Video for ‘Expectations’ Remix
description: Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan appear on vintage game shows in the retro music video for the “Expectations” remix, featuring appearances from mus
body:
Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan appear on vintage game shows in the retro music video for the “Expectations” remix, featuring appearances from musician David Byrne and producer Dan Nigro.

	The clip, directed by Bardia Zeinali, shows Rodrigo and Roan (in her first-ever feature) appearing on sets clearly inspired by “Family Feud” and “Hollywood Squares.” Byrne appears as Johnny Johnson, host of the “Big Expectations” show, where he asks three Rodrigos in different outfits “a little bit how you got here.”
	



	What follows is a trip to the different sets and a new “Expectations” verse from Roan, who shows up on the set of “Sister Squabble” to contend with Rodrigo in a “Family Feud” face-off. “I took her to a concert front row thought it’d be fun,” she sings. “Her hand moving up my skirt, no piercing on her tongue / She said she’d call me later, that was three weeks ago / Classic L.A. behavior, she could’ve just said no.”


	Nigro, who produced “Expectations” along with Roan and Rodrigo’s albums, pops up at the end clutching a giant brick of a phone straight out of the 1990s. His appearance makes sense, as he produced the track and its parent album “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love.”

	Speaking to Apple Music’s Zane Lowe on Thursday afternoon, Roan and Rodrigo explained why they teamed for the remix. “This is obviously my first feature,” said Roan. “I’ve never done this before, so it feels perfect to me. I don’t know. I feel like it represents a generation of songwriters that are just really thinking about their lyrics. I felt like with this song, I was like, ‘Wow, it’s so cool that she is putting a pretty difficult concept within the pop song,’ which is my favorite pop songs ever.”
	

	Rodrigo explained that she had asked Byrne to appear in the video but was a “bit sheepish” about making the request. “I always feel shy asking people for favors, but he was so down,” she said. “He showed up the entire day. He had a character that he had built out and he made this Johnny Johnson character. There’s so many outtakes we have of him just improvising and riffing and he was so into it. And I was like, ‘Gosh, David, maybe he should be an actor too one of these days.” He’s very multi-talented.”

	Beyond sharing Nigro as a producer, Rodrigo and Roan go back some years, as the latter supported the former on both her “Sour” and “Guts” tours. Roan recently performed at Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival in late August as part of an all-female lineup that featured Doechii, Rachel Chinouriri, Garbage, the Breeders and more.

title: Jenna Ortega Says She Hopes ‘Klara and the Sun’ Encourages People to ‘Put Down the Computers and Phones’ as Dystopian Film World Premieres in London
description: Jenna Ortega hopes that her new film, the dystopian sci-fi “Klara and the Sun,” can remind people to live in the moment in the age of AI and all-co
body:
Jenna Ortega hopes that her new film, the dystopian sci-fi “Klara and the Sun,” can remind people to live in the moment in the age of AI and all-consuming technology. 

	“I think we gotta put our focus on one another and put down the computers and phones,” the star told Variety on the red carpet at the movie’s world premiere at London Film Festival on Thursday night.

	Ortega, wearing a stunning yellow lace dress and hair piece, added: “Remember to be present and to appreciate people while they’re standing right in front of you.”
	

	Based on Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling 2021 novel of the same name, “Klara and the Sun” is set in a future where advances in genetic engineering have divided humans into strict social classes. Ortega plays Klara, an artificial android companion who is purchased for an ailing girl named Josie (Mia Tharia). “Klara and the Sun” is directed by “Thor” helmer Taika Waititi and also stars Amy Adams as Josie’s mother, Aran Murphy (son of Cillian Murphy), Natasha Lyonne, Steve Buscemi and more.


	Waititi, Adams, Murphy and Lyonne all walked the London Film Festival red carpet on Thursday night, alongside Waititi’s wife Rita Ora, author Ishiguro and a surprise appearance from Florence Pugh, who stunned in a blue floral gown with statement sleeves. Pugh enthusiastically greeted Ortega and Adams before they all posed for photos together alongside producer Rachel Forman.



	

					Florence Pugh, Amy Adams, Jenna Ortega and Rachel Forman at the “Klara and the Sun” world premiere in London.
									Getty Images for BFI
	



	Standing alongside Ortega, Adams added that everyone she’s spoken to has gotten “something different” out of the film. “That, to me, is a really successful film that communicates something different to each viewer. So I like hearing what people get out of it,” she said.
	

	Ortega clarified that though Klara is an “artificial friend,” she doesn’t work like the AI that we know today.

	“AI I guess pulls all this information from the internet and Klara gets all her information from the real world,” she said. “So that’s a little bit different. She’s kind of like a toddler in a sense. Playing her specifically in this film was really interesting because Taika wanted a more human approach, so he didn’t want to do movement that was too robotic, maybe more sort of clumsy and unknowing.”

	Waititi echoed Ortega in saying that the film’s message is to “put the phone down.” 

	“I would just like people to remember what friendship is, connect with people and just be,” he said. “Just be in the moment.”  

	Ishiguro acknowledged that, since his novel came out in 2021, the world’s awareness and attitude about AI has changed greatly.

	“This film doesn’t address a lot of the anxieties that you and I may have right now about where we’re going with the technology. I mean, I think quite rightly, it’s really come center stage,” he said. “I’m aware that this film is coming out into a very different world to the one that my novel came out in five years ago, and I don’t know how that will change people’s expectations or how people look at things. But I’ll say that this isn’t another film about how an AI machine seems to be nice and then becomes sinister and ends up killing all the nice people in the film. It’s not that sort of story.” 

	Ishiguro is wading more into film, confirming to Variety that he’s working on a new project with Tim Burton, for which he penned an original script. Though Burton and Ishiguro have a mutual friend in “Wednesday” star Ortega, he said she’s not the one who introduced them. 

	“I thought this was supposed to be a big secret!” Ishiguro said. “No, Jenna didn’t introduce us. Tim lives quite near where I live in North London, and I was dropping in on him in his very strange and wacky and beautiful house. I mean, it looks like a Tim Burton set. And we started to talk about a project and I wrote a script on spec. We decided to just do it privately between the two of us, and then take it to people.” 

	He added that it’s not a “war film,” saying: “Genre-wise, it’s very hard to pigeonhole. It’s a Tim Burton film!”
	

	“Klara and the Sun” is set to hit theaters via Sony Pictures on Oct. 23.

title: Why Did Netflix Boot Bela Bajaria?
description: Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer.Yes
body:
Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer.Yes, the company that popularized the “Keeper Test” is known for abrupt exits. But despite Netflix’s recent stock struggles, many considered Bajaria too big to fail.Word of her ouster leaked before the executive had the chance to address most of her internal teams — an announcement dovetailed with news of her incoming replacement, the venerated film and TV executive Peter Rice. As the former general entertainment chairman of the Walt Disney Company, Rice’s bona fides are clear — “I wish I bought stock this morning,” one huge talent rep said about Netflix’s new hire — but it doesn’t explain how Bajaria fell out of favor so fast.One word that came up in nearly a dozen conversations with industry players this afternoon about Bajaria’s pink-slipping: “scapegoat.”Netflix is obviously against the ropes again, after slowing user engagement on the service rattled Wall Street investors and layoffs came this week as a sacrifice to the share price. But Bajaria’s dismissal makes it clear, according to the numerous sources we spoke with, that content is once again going to take it on the chin.“People always blame the content,” said the source, “but you don’t lay off 1,000 people unless there’s a big problem with the business model.”Bajaria’s exit echoes similarly shocking removals in Netflix history — notably that of Cindy Holland, the company’s first content queen who oversaw flagship hits like “House of Cards,” “Stranger Things” and “The Crown.” Holland was ousted in 2020, when Sarandos combined English-language and international content under Bajaria (elevating the latter to the largest autonomous content job in the streamer’s history).Holland, one insider with knowledge of Netflix observed to Variety, built a business of boutique hits. Bajaria’s foresight was sharper, investing in local language productions and building up Netflix’s global presence (almost two dozen international offices were opened during Bajaria’s reign). She is also credited internally with pushing the streamer into live entertainment. Bajaria was on the “ground floor” of licensing deals with WWE and the NFL, which have proven significant draws for the ad-supported tier of Netflix subscribers, per the source. Her talent relations were on par with others at her level (Bajaria was ubiquitous at premieres and launches in film and TV, most recently at Sarandos’ side at the L.A. premiere of Ben Affleck’s “Animals”).“The problem isn’t engagement,” said yet another person with knowledge of Netflix. “It’s that the only lever to pull for revenue growth is raising the subscriber price. How’s that Bela’s problem? Where’s the CFO and the CEO?”Interestingly, we hear that Rice came into play only a few weeks ago when he was reported to be interviewing with Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz for a top position at that newly combined company. The lunch meeting, one source familiar with the men said, was called so Kreiz could request that Rice replace him on the board of his former company Mattel. Regardless, it alerted the town that Rice was done with semi-retirement (a producing deal with A24) and ready to come back to a big job. Another hot Thursday rumor said that Rice also met recently with NBCUniversal about a post there. One source familiar with NBCU said there was no job in play for Rice under Donna Langley’s expansive umbrella, so it’s unclear what he would’ve met about. A spokesperson for NBCUniversal had no comment.Another lunch may have proven consequential in Bajaria’s exit. Earlier this year, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was spotted breaking bread with HBO chief content officer Casey Bloys. Was Sarandos courting Bloys for a top job at the streamer, perhaps to take the job then held by Bajaria? Soon, the spin machine reframed the meeting as a friendly gathering, floating the idea that it was a pitch for Bloys to sign a production deal under Bajaria if he did not want to find a way to work at the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. At a Bloomberg conference last week, Sarandos downplayed the meeting: “He’s a good guy,” he said about Bloys. “For some reason, we had a very well-publicized lunch.”Perhaps. But in hindsight, now that Sarandos has leveled the ax on Bajaria after 10 years, is a lunch ever really just a meal? Rice’s recent focus has been as the head of ceremonies and content for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games — but now Rice focuses on a more urgent task. The exec has been on the open market in the years since he was let go at Disney. He’s seen as the rare exec who has spent time heading up both major film and TV businesses, so the job of chief content officer at Netflix, where he’ll oversee both, makes sense. He’s also well-liked and respected from his time at 20th Century Fox, heading up Fox Searchlight and later the Fox network, and eventually becoming president of parent company 21st Century Fox prior to Disney’s acquisition.“Surprise” was also a common refrain both inside and out of Netflix on Thursday about the turn of events. But a few hints had already been out there: Netflix is set to report its Q3 earnings next Tuesday, so such a move would have to be made beforehand. And with co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters not going anywhere, the sacrificial lamb next in line was Bajaria. Observers speculated that the Q3 results are likely to be extremely disappointing for the streamer, which is already facing some tough headwinds.At that same Screentime event, anyone reading between the lines might have guessed that Sarandos was getting antsy with Netflix’s current low-growth status. In particular, he was asked about Netflix’s slower growth (2% year-over-year growth in user engagement during the first half in 2026). “Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said. Turns out Bajaria’s exit was a part of that change. Now all eyes turn to Rice’s plans for Netflix, and whether those plans will include some of Bajaria’s lieutenants, such as U.S./Canada head of scripted series Jinny Howe and film lead Dan Lin.Bajaria may also have hit thin ice with Sarandos after the streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy Awards this year — its worst showing since 2016 and down from 30 in 2025. That’s quite a turn from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44.Along with the Emmy slump, Netflix hasn’t premiered a culture-defining hit in the vein of “Stranger Things” in quite some time. But it’s still fielded some of the most-watched programs of the year, including “His & Hers” and Season 4 of “Bridgerton.” Bajaria is known for her keen creative eye, honed over the years at places like CBS and NBCUniversal (where she was ultimately head of Universal TV before moving to Netflix in 2016).“In her decade at Netflix, Bela’s impact has been undeniable — from attracting new talent, bringing live sports, concerts and events to driving the company’s global expansion and push into new areas of entertainment,” WME co-chair Richard Weitz tells Variety. “Her relationships with talent have been integral in Netflix’s relationships with A talent across the platform. Simply put, she’s been transformational and I know her worldwide team and the talent who have worked with her will miss her.”Rice will not inherit a bus of happy campers. He’ll have to galvanize a team that lost a slew of executives Wednesday as a result of pink slips; on the TV side, that included Carolina Garcia, who has been let go as director of original series after a decade with the streamer.as well as scheduling head Andy Kubitz, Lisa Lang McMullen (director, overall deals, series), Andrew McQuinn (director, original series), James Oh (director, original drama series) and Jason Pan (manager, original series creative development).

	The remaining film group appears safe for now, as Lin’s team saw a major sacrifice in VP Doug Belgrad earlier this week. Morale will need tweaking, budgets adjusting and a slew of new lunches will be scheduled. What you can count on, per one of the streaming insiders, is that “eventually, everyone’s time comes at Netflix.”

title: Steven Soderbergh to Help Finish ‘The Batman 2’ Filming After Matt Reeves Stepped Away for Family Matter
description: Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help complete “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves is on hiatus dealing with a personal matter, Vari
body:
Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help complete “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves is on hiatus dealing with a personal matter, Variety has confirmed.

	“As Matt Reeves continues to attend to an ongoing family matter, Steven Soderbergh, as an admirer of Matt’s work, approached Matt and will step in, with the full support of DC Studios, to help the writer-director complete the final weeks of principal photography on ‘The Batman Part 2,'” a studio rep said in a statement. “Matt and Steven will work closely together with the actors and crew to fulfill Matt’s vision of the film.”
	

	Soderbergh said in his own statement, “I thought Matt Reeves’ work on ‘The Batman’ was stunning; it was intentional, specific and rigorously coherent. The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.” 


	Reeves clarified on X that he will still be working on the production, just not on the set while principal photography wraps up. 

Just to be clear, I am not leaving The Batman Part II. I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes. 🦇— Matt Reeves (@mattreevesLA) October 15, 2026


	Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced “The Batman Part II” production pause in early October, stating that Reeves temporarily stepped away from the project to handle a “family matter.” 

	“Production on ‘The Batman Part II’ has been temporarily paused while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter,” a rep said in a statement at the time. “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.”

	Soderbergh is the Oscar-winning director best known for films “Traffic,” “Erin Brockovich,” “Sex, Lies, and Videotape and “Ocean’s Eleven.” His most recent releases include “The Christophers,” “Black Bag,” “Presence” and “John Lennon: The Last Interview.”
	

	The highly anticipated “Batman” sequel has experienced several delays since it was announced at CinemaCon 2022. The original release date was set for Oct. 2, 2026, before Warner Bros. delayed it to Oct. 1, 2027. In June, the film was pushed again to February 2028. Reeves’ first “Batman” was released in March 2022.

	Robert Pattinson returns as the Caped Crusader in “The Batman Part II.” Other cast members include Scarlett Johansson, Colin Farrell, Sebastian Stan, Andy Serkis and Jeffrey Wright.

title: ‘Fourth Wing’ TV Series Casts Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya as Violet Sorrengail and Xaden Riorson

body:
“Fourth Wing,” Amazon Prime Video’s TV adaptation of Rebecca Yarros’ bestselling romantasy series, has found its leads.

	Esther McGregor has been cast in the role of Violet Sorrengail while Emilio Sakraya will play Xaden Riorson, Variety has learned. Amazon declined comment.

	McGregor is best known for starring as Mirren Sinclair Sheffield in Amazon’s “We Were Liars,” with previous credits including Disney+’s “Obi-Wan Kenobi” and Freevee’s “High School.” Up next, she stars in the Amazon series “Life Is Strange.”
	

	Sakraya has a hefty list of credits in both TV and film from his native Germany as well as in the U.S.; his credits include “Rhinegold,” “Tribes of Europa” and “Warrior Nun.” His other recent projects include “Those About to Die,” and he’s set to appear in Season 3 of “One Piece.”


	“Fourth Wing” is set inside the brutal world of Basgiath War College, where there is only one rule: graduate or die. Twenty-year-old Violet Sorrengail was always expected to live a quiet life — but she’s sent on an entirely different path when her mother, a general in the military, orders her to join the hundreds of candidates striving to become dragon riders, the elite of Navarre.

	Starting with the release of New York Times bestseller “Fourth Wing” in May 2023, Yarros’ “The Empyrean” book series currently includes sequels “Iron Flame” (November 2023) and “Onyx Storm” (January 2025.) This September, Yarros released the novella “Threshing Day,” which tells 13 stories set in the “The Empyrean” universe. The titles and release dates for the planned fourth and fifth books have yet to be announced.
	

	Ordered to series at Amazon in May, Meredith Averill (“Anne With an E”) is showrunner and executive producer of “Fourth Wing.” The show is also executive produced by Kilter Films (Lisa Joy — who also directs the pilot, Jonathan Nolan and Athena Wickham), Outlier Society (Michael B. Jordan and Elizabeth Raposo) and Premeditated Productions (Liz Pelletier and Sherryl Clark).

title: The Most Shocking Thing About ‘You Can See Everything’: Nathan Fielder’s Sympathy for the Devil
description: Ever since the first trailer went up for “You Can See Everything,” if not since word of the movie got up, schadenfreude lovers have been rubbing th
body:
Ever since the first trailer went up for “You Can See Everything,” if not since word of the movie got up, schadenfreude lovers have been rubbing their hands with glee at the prospect of Elizabeth Holmes getting more of what’s coming to her. Especially knowing that Holmes and her husband Billy Evans actually sought out Nathan Fielder, who exudes a natural skepticism, to make the documentary, there’s been an anticipatory bloodlust, that they must have been fools to imagine they were doing anything but helping set their own trap. That’s not a completely ill-founded expectation: Holmes comes off in the doc as every bit as innately bizarre as anyone showing up for a cinematic freak show might hope. But the weirdest thing about the movie might be the fact that it at least allows for the possibility that the Evil Genius might be neither of the things contained in that descriptor, but rather somebody whose guileless act may not be that much of a put-on, because she’s dealing with some kind of mysterious damage we can only begin to guess at.
	

	In other words, it’s a movie with some sympathy for the devil, or at least — given the admitted inconclusiveness of its findings — the suggestion that empathy may be possible. Which may be not what you’re expecting walking in to what looks like a hilarious 174-minute takedown. But the intentions of Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim, are embedded right in that first trailer that set the watching world ablaze. At the scene’s very end, when after a couple of minutes of Holmes smiling and staring earnestly into the narrator’s eyes, with a shaky head that makes it appear as if she’s developed some kind of anxious palsy, it’s revealed that she’s extending her left leg well off the couch to rock her baby. If you were watching that teaser carefully, the filmmakers were carefully signaling the whole movie: vast amounts of IRL comedic shock and awe, tinged with lingering bits of poignance as Holmes turns out to be a human being… if a still-unfathomable one.
	

	So, let’s set a countdown for how long it takes for some souls on social media to begin calling Fielder a “cuck,” for having fallen prey to the manipulation of an obvious villain. But it’s not a movie that means to let Holmes off any hooks, only to ask some questions about where some of the invisible hooks in her impossibly strange life might lie. It’s a film that starts off with the intent to provide insight into a Leonard Nimoy- or Robert Stack-style unsolved-mystery episode, with the idea that spending 34 days living with Holmes and Evans — and years of further production beyond her incarceration — would surely have to provide a few concrete conclusions about her psychology and/or crimes. Instead, by the end, it makes solving the puzzle of UFOs seem like a cinch by comparison. Abnormal psychology: it’s the Ultimate Trip! But the idea that, amid that inability to form answers, we could at least further consider what makes her tick will seem risible and outrageous to some viewers… and is also what makes the film rich and re-visitable enough to deserve the Best Picture nomination it’s clearly lined up to get.

	If there’s a great crux moment for the movie, it’s in the scene fairly late in the three-hour proceedings that involve a sort of postmortem between Fielder and the Very Famous A-List Personality whose appearance A24 has asked viewers to consider a spoiler. (Her name will be ubiquitous enough in the weeks to come, but we can honor the surprise for now.) Fielder confesses how confused he is, after spending months doing intensive filming of Holmes and her husband and immediate family — basically wondering if, against all odds, it is possible that she could be as guileless as she comes off 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Upon hearing that confession, the Very Famous A-List Personality does everything but literally slap Fielder, suggesting that he must be experiencing some kind of Stockholm Syndrome to have been pulled in by her act. At this, some filmgoers will be practically standing up and cheering for the A-lister — she has at that moment become the audience’s surrogate, or stand-in for at least part of it, urging the host/filmmaker to snap out of his delirium. But it won’t just be different viewers taking sides in this scene. It may be anyone watching the movie whose empathic and cynical sides are in roughly equal balance.
	

	Where Fielder ultimately ended up on the issue of how sincere or Machiavellian Holmes is another unsolved mystery at the end of the movie, perhaps even to himself. When I caught the film at its Telluride Film Festival premiere (followed by a Q&A attendees weren’t allowed to record), Fielder basically said that he and others on the filmmaking team still had trouble figuring out exactly what they’d experienced in the process of making the movie — which is a fascinating conundrum, considering that, true to its title, Holmes and her husband did let them see just about everything it seemed possible to see. My personal hunch is that Fielder came away thinking Holmes is on the level, to the extent that someone who sometimes seems like an AI program’s idea of how a human should behave can be on the level. There are a few possibilities that might explain how Holmes comes off the way she does in the movie: (a) She is a simpleton. (b) She is a conniving sociopath who happens to be utterly brilliant at playing a simpleton. (c) Somewhere between those poles, she is the very emblem of a woman who throughout her life has put herself in the sway of controlling men, to the detriment of her intellect, willpower and emotional development.

	And what about those impossibly wide, unblinking eyes, and that gentle Joker smile? Are these the hallmarks, as I’ve seen theorized throughout the internet, of someone who is deeply sociopathic at worst, or on the scale at best? Or just someone with Resting Beatific Face?

	The sort of feminist lens is a powerful one, if you choose to go down that path of interpretation. Fielder and Oppenheim include a moment early in the film in which Holmes’ father blurts out that he believes things really started to change for his daughter when she was raped in her college days. On-camera, Fielder offers one of the quietly startled reaction shots that are a staple of the movie, and the topic never comes up again. The theme of her becoming the victim of powerful men continues — a little bit when the subject of Theranos co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani comes up (although recounting past history doesn’t take up much of this doc’s running time), and a lot when we get to the present day. Evans is as close as “You Can See Everything” has to a villain, and probably crosses the line into counting as one. Even he is treated as a rounded human being over the course of the film; he’s too candid and open about ihs intentions to count as a top-level devil, and it seems like he might actually love Holmes. But the succession of constant revelations about what he’s up to in the last hour of the movie make Holmes feel like a woman with virtually no personal agency, even before she goes to jail, let alone afterward, when he is making deals without her knowledge and keeping up a cocky, profane tweetstorm under her name that bears scant resemblance to her personality as we know it.
	

	It may be not giving Holmes nearly enough credit for her misdeeds to suggest that she has actually spent most of her adult years as a puppet. Yet the portrait of her passivity in the face of an aggressive “let me handle everything” man never stops growing more startling as the film goes on… and has to feel at least a little real for anyone with much first-hand human-race experience.

	Two scenes that explore Holmes’ seeming — and shocking — naivete stand out. (Neither of these count as major “plot” spoilers.) One comes early on when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied, and when she says no, he asks the inevitable what-about-white-lies question. Even then, it’s a no, as Fielder almost begs her to admit that she understands the question and has told a fib or two to protect a friend’s feelings. Probably 99.99% of the population would surrender at the point — evil geniuses most of all — but Holmes can’t admit to even having falsely complimented a pal. Later on, there’s a mind-blowing scene in which Fielder uses the historically famous Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” sketch as a setup to explore how people’s communication paths might just blow right by each other. Holmes hasn’t heard of the skit, but after watching it, she says she sees what he’s trying to say… which itself turns out to be a white lie, because she finally admits that she just doesn’t get what’s going on between Abbott and Costello, at all. And it’s at this point that you might start to wonder if she is just developmentally disabled in some way.

	Stunted in her growth, somehow, yet capable of convincing smart people to part with billions of dollars? Something here does not compute. And yet, intuitively, Holmes does not come off in this movie as someone with the kind of intellectual cunning to pretend not to understand an Abbott and Costello sketch that has entertained millions, or to not know what a white lie is. The enigma deepens.

	But so does the possibility that, for all her sins, and for all her Stanford education, Holmes is a simple gal — not simpleton — suffering from an extreme case of not just serial male dominance but terminal Imposters’ Syndrome. (Which is something that, from the available evidence in the movie, she surely would not admit to, not least of all because she might never have heard of it.)
	

	How people feel about Holmes after watching “You Can See Everything” might be the most divisive thing in America since… well, since Kelly Clarkson versus the Brooklyn boutique, the thing that has truly riven us as a nation. But one thing is clear: In this era of ever-shortening quick hits and hot takes, Fielder and Oppenheim’s luxuriously paced peering into someone’s soul feels like a balm, inconclusive or not. Is it possible that the more you learn about someone, the less you might know how to think about them?

	To take a cue from Shakespeare: “You Can See Everything” suggests that there are more things in the heaven and earth that is just one person than are dreamt of in any of our philosophies. We could do worse than to have the possibility of sympathy thrown in amid those hours of head-scratching assessment.

	(By the way, who is on first…)

title: Netflix Shocker: Bela Bajaria Leaving After 10 Years Amid Layoffs, Peter Rice to Replace as Chief Content Officer
description: In a major executive shake-up, Bela Bajaria is out at Netflix after 10 years at the streamer, most recently serving as its chief content officer.
body:
In a major executive shake-up, Bela Bajaria is out at Netflix after 10 years at the streamer, most recently serving as its chief content officer.

	She will be replaced by former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice, as first reported by Puck. As chief content officer, Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions.


	Bajaria’s exit comes amid a significant workforce reduction at Netflix. Around 1,000 employees (6% of the company) were laid off this week in what marks the streamer’s largest axing to date. Netflix’s film VP Doug Belgrad and film director Sheroum Kim were also pink slipped as part of the restructuring.
	

	“I want to thank Bela for a decade of dedication, innovation, creativity and leadership,” Sarandos, Netflix’s co-CEO, said in a statement. “She led enormous changes at Netflix. She helped broaden our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports, in addition to crafting and running a world class, global slate of films and series. I’m incredibly grateful for everything she’s done to help Netflix entertain the world.”

	Bajaria joined Netflix in 2016 after she was let go from NBCUniversal, where she had served as president of Universal Television. In that role, she had produced shows that aired on Netflix, including “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” and “Master of None.” Sarandos first brought in Bajaria to help Netflix launch an unscripted division, as well as licensing and studio co-productions. Bajaria was later elevated to head of global in 2020 as Cindy Holland exited the company, and was named chief content officer in January 2023.
	

	Under her watch, Bajaria oversaw popular TV series including “Bridgerton,” “Squid Game,” “Adolescence,” “Beef,” “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” and films such as “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Frankenstein.” She also pushed Netflix into more live sports and events like “The Roast of Tom Brady” and deals with the NFL and WWE.

	But in recent months, as Netflix growth has slowed, so too has the aura around its original programming. The streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy Awards this year — down from 30 in 2025 and quite a distance from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44. All told, 2026 was Netflix’s lowest Primetime Emmy haul since 2016.

	“I know this is a big change in a year that has already had its share,” Sarandos wrote in a memo to staff. “But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN [United States and Canada] where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world.

	Rice’s own ousting at Disney in 2022, by then-CEO Bob Chapek, was a huge shock to the industry given his stature at the company. A well-regarded executive with strong talent relations, Rice was most recently chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the Walt Disney Company. There he oversaw ABC, FOX Broadcasting, Fox Sports, ABC News, ABC Studios, Disney Channel, Freeform, FX Networks, Hulu, National Geographic, Onyx Collective, Disney Television and Twentieth Century Fox Television, with more than 300 shows and 4,000 hours of television a year. Programs during his tenure included “The Simpsons,” “American Idol,” “Modern Family,” “This Is Us,” “The Bear,” “Abbott Elementary,” “Shogun” and “Only Murders in the Building,” along with ABC News programming and sporting events such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup Finals. 

	Since he was let go from Disney, Rice worked as a producer on movies such as Jason Reitman’s “Saturday Night,” “28 Years Later” and “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” at Sony, as well as “Warfare” and Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” at A24. He is currently producing Alex Garland’s “Elden Ring” and Sonoya Mizuno’s “Stages,” as well as well as the opening and closing ceremonies for the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
	

	Earlier in his career, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group, and Fox’s lead executive on the Hulu board. He also headed Fox Searchlight Pictures where he shepherded indie favorites like “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Juno,” “Little Miss Sunshine” and “Sideways.”

	“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across TV and film is deep and broad,” Sarandos said. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives. I’m excited to welcome him to Netflix as chief content officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love.”

	Added Rice, “Netflix has fundamentally changed the way stories are made, shared and experienced around the world. They’ve shown again and again that they’re willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I’m excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere.”

	Mike Schneider contributed to this report.

title: Taylor Sheridan’s ‘Frisco King’ Starring Samuel L. Jackson Sets Release Date (TV News Roundup)
description: Samuel L. Jackson is the new returning king in town in Taylor Sheridan’s “Frisco King,” where he reprises his role of Russell Lee Washington Jr..
body:
Samuel L. Jackson is the new returning king in town in Taylor Sheridan’s “Frisco King,” where he reprises his role of Russell Lee Washington Jr..

	The New Orleans gangster establishes a new kingdom in Frisco, Texas, where he discovers a hustler running his business amid the suburban town. Per the series logline, “Recruiting an ambitious protégé, a loyal driver and a growing network of eccentric partners, Lee transforms small hustles into big business. But, every new score raises the stakes, and as his influence grows, so do the risks, forcing Lee to stay one grift ahead. Frisco may not know it yet, but its new king has arrived.”
	

	The series will premiere on Paramount+ Dec. 18 with two episodes, followed by new episodes weekly. Starring alongside Jackson are Asa Germann, Kai Caster, Lilah Pate and Savanna Gann, with a special appearance by Sylvester Stallone.


	Written by Sheridan, “Frisco King” is executive produced by Stallone, Jackson, Sheridan, David C. Glasser, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, LaTanya Richardson Jackson and Keith Cox. Christina Alexandra Voros and Michael Friedman executive produce in addition to both directing four episodes, with Voros directing the pilot. The series is produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios,

	Watch the teaser for “Frisco King” below.



	In other TV roundup news:
	
		Specials	

	CBS set “The Price is Right at Night: Live Holiday Special” and “The Price is Right: 20 Seasons of Drew Carey” to air in December.

	“The Price is Right at Night: Live Holiday Special” will premiere on Dec. 13 at 8 p.m. ET on CBS. The broadcast marks the first time television’s longest-running game show will air in real time. Viewers will also get behind-the-scenes access with host Drew Carey, announcer George Gray, the models and the production team as they race to keep the show on track.
	

	On Dec. 15, CBS will air “The Price is Right: 20 Seasons of Drew Carey.” The special will celebrate two decades of Carey as host, featuring celebrity appearances from previous episodes including Mila Kunis, Jack Black and Snoop Dogg.

	The live holiday special is produced by Fremantle, with John Quinn as showrunner and executive producer. The Drew Carey special is produced by Fremantle, with James Davis and Quinn as executive producers. Both specials will be available to stream on Paramount+.
	
		Initiatives	

	FilAm Creative announced its inaugural TV Creator Lab cohort of 25 writers.

	The tuition-free, five-month program is designed to help emerging television creators develop their original scripted series. The selected writers will learn from working television executives, producers, showrunners and industry professionals.

	The Lab launched Oct. 8 at Patriot Pictures in Los Angeles. The cohort gathered for a conversation with Lionsgate SVP of Television Richard Rothschild, Greg Coolidge (“The Continental: From the World of John Wick”) and Oren Segal, moderated by television director Francis dela Torre (“Almost Paradise”).

	The writers selected are Angel Cielo, Candice Sarangay, Celena Cipriaso, Eileen Cabiling, Ella Espiritu, Eric J. De La Rosa, Eugene Ramos, Faith Christy Soliven, Frances Rubio, Geri Carillo, Hermie Castillo, Jaime Estepa, Jalen Giovanni Jones, Joshua Labata, Joy Regullano, Kim Marcelino, Nicole Wolf, Noël Wiggins, Rebecca Williams Spindler, Roann Enriquez, Rommel Rojas, Stacie Gancayco-Adlao, Teodorico Sajor, Walter Boholst and Yasmine Gomez.

	*

	The American Film Institute announced the mentors for its 2026 Writers’ Room Ready program.

	This year’s mentors are Brad Ingelsby (“Task,” “Mare of Easttown”), Peter Gould (“Better Call Saul,” “Breaking Bad”) Patrik-Ian Polk (“Noah’s Arc,” “P-Valley”), Sev Ohanian (“Sinners,” “Searching”) and Sarah-Violet Bliss (“Scorn,” “Search Party”).

	The creatives will be paired with AFI Class of 2025 graduates:Brad Ingelsby with Nathan Bouton — “Black Tide,” one-hour dramaPeter Gould with Kirby Saxton — “Holy Water,” half-hour comedyPatrik-Ian Polk with Chri’shawn Julius — “Pop Puss,” half-hour comedySev Ohanian with Edward Nenedzhyan — “The Optic,” one-hour dramaSarah-Violet Bliss with Annabel Newland — “Glitter,” half-hour comedy
	

	“Great writing is taught in community, not isolation,” said Susan Ruskin, AFI Conservatory dean and executive vice president of the American Film Institute. “We are deeply grateful to our accomplished mentors, whose wisdom, expertise and generosity empower our Writers’ Room Ready participants to transform their potential into professional practice in the industry.”

	The Writers’ Room Ready program recognizes outstanding original television pilot scripts written by AFI Conservatory Screenwriting Fellows.
	
		Partnerships 	

	Elmo and his “Sesame Street” friends are taking on an African safari adventure in a special PBS ‘Nature’ primetime crossover. “Sesame Street and the Great Elephant Adventure” premieres on Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 8 p.m. ET on PBS and PBS Kids and will stream on pbs.org/nature, YouTube,pbskids.org, the PBS KIDS Video app and the PBS app.

	Per the release, “The adventure begins at the group’s safari lodge, where they meet the lodge manager and her young daughter, who introduce Elmo and Abby to Kenya’s culture, nature and wildlife. Along the way, Elmo struggles with the idea of leaving his adopted elephant behind but comes to learn that the greatest way to care for his new friend is to let her thrive where she belongs: in the wild.”

	“Bringing Elmo and the ‘Sesame Street’ friends into the world of ‘Nature’ allows us to tell a unique story filled with adventure, discovery, and heart,” Sal Perez, executive producer for Sesame Workshop, said. “We hope this special event sparks curiosity in children and encourages them to see themselves as explorers and problem solvers, while reminding viewers of every age that some of life’s greatest lessons come from experiencing nature.”
	
		Programming	

	Moonbug Entertainment announced that actress and performer Lauren Vaz will join Cashaé Monya in playing Meekah in the global “Blippi” franchise.

	“Lauren brings such a natural warmth, confidence and sense of fun to Meekah,” Liz Katz, Associate General Manager of “Blippi” and lead of the Meekah franchise, said. “She really captures the curiosity and big-sister energy that families know and love about Meekah. We’re so excited to welcome her to our ensemble cast alongside Cashaé Monya as we enter an exciting new chapter for Meekah, with more to share in the weeks ahead.”
	

	“Blippi” is a live-action kids’ franchise built around curiosity, exploration and real-world adventures. Meekah is an established character who can be brought to life by different performers. Vaz now joins Monya in sharing the role across the Blippi franchise, as Meekah prepares to enter an exciting new chapter.

	“Getting to step into Meekah’s shoes is incredibly special to me,” Vaz said. “I love how she encourages kids to be curious, express themselves and have the confidence to jump in and try something new. Having already been part of the Blippi world on tour, I’m so excited to continue this journey with Meekah and bring my personality, creativity and sense of fun to all the adventures ahead.”
	
		Executive News	

	Hearst Media Production Group named Amy DeGregorio as executive vice president of sales and revenue.

	In the newly created role, DeGregorio will act as a key member of HMPG’s executive team and strategic advisor to the company’s president on revenue growth, commercialization and new business opportunities. She will be responsible for driving revenue strategy and overseeing sales and sponsorship activity.

	Prior to her new role, DeGregorio served as senior vice president, managing director of sales for educational/informational programming for HMPG since 2022.

	“Amy has done an exceptional job building meaningful brand partnerships and seamlessly integrating sponsors into our E/I programming,” said Bryan Curb, HMPG president. “As HMPG continues to expand, we want to bring that same expertise and strategic approach to our entire portfolio, creating new opportunities for brands to engage with our award-winning content and loyal audiences.”

	In 2016, DeGregorio joined Litton Entertainment, which was rebranded to HMPG in 2022, as senior director, integrated marketing. She was promoted to vice president, integrated marketing and, in 2020, senior vice president, client solutions. Before joining Litton, she worked at CBS Television Stations, and has held roles at NBCUniversal, truTV, ABC Television and MTV Networks.

title: The 27 Best ‘American Horror Story’ Characters, Ranked
description:

body:
Oct 15, 2026 5:00pm PT	
	




			
			
	
						

									Courtesy of FX
	
					


							
		

	“American Horror Story” has given audiences a lot to chew on over the years: wildly inventive themes, sadistic imagery, over-the-top performances and gleefully macabre mythology.

	But arguably its greatest contribution to television since its debut in 2011 is its characters, an ever-expanding company of ill-fated spooks and kooks who rarely find a happy ending, and yet we relish in watching their descent into whatever brand of hell the series is conjuring that season. The citizens of this connected universe of horror storytelling, from creators Ryan Murphy and Brad Fulchuk, are ultimately what stitch it all together, and have proven to be the enduring draw for audiences left wanting more from their favorites.

	For its 13th season, “AHS” has banked on the bedrock of those characters by dipping back into its stable of actors and their alter egos for a mashup season. The satanic-centric story has been a chaotic exercise in fan service, with varying degrees of success. When it works, there are undeniable pleasures in seeing characters thought to be done and dusted come back for one more shot at a good line reading or an uncanny interaction with someone who shares their face. Many of those characters are on this list, some elevated by the extra screen time and some demoted for disrupting a previously perfect storyline.

	As “AHS” plays the hits for 13, let’s rank the best characters from the series. The following list isn’t necessarily a grading of performance, but rather character arc, impact and sheer entertainment value. It should also be noted that “AHS13” focuses almost exclusively on characters from the first eight seasons, with good reason. Even for their flaws, those characters are the series’ best work. More recent seasons were considered for this list, but frankly, “AHS” hasn’t aged all that well –– even though some of its characters have.


			
			
	Coco St. Pierre Vanderbilt (Leslie Grossman)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Grossman has been making a meal out of Murphy-scripted roles since she appeared on “Popular,” his first series, as Mary Cherry, so “AHS” is better off with her among its ranks. But she doesn’t get enough credit for taking so-so characters within this world and really making them sing — or scream. Take Coco St. Pierre, a Beverly Hills-bred socialite who thinks she has survived the “Apocalypse” only to learn she is really a mind-wiped witch hidden right under the nose of the Antichrist. But her power is the ability to detect gluten, and that’s not a joke. She’s a witch who believes she has nothing to provide her coven. Rather, she functions as a supportive sister who contributes to morale as much as magic, until her time comes. Stay with us here, because in “AHS13,” Coco uses her gluten spidey sense to take down the Zodiac killer by inducing diabetic shock. None of those words have ever been spoken together before, so Coco deserves her flowers for making history.
		
			
			
	Montana Duke (Billie Lourd)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Lourd has played a number of major roles in “AHS,” chief among them Mallory, one of its most powerful, if not the most powerful, witch. But with all due respect to that character, Lourd has never been more fun than when she was trying on the bleached blonde wig of Montana Duke, the aerobics instructor turned right hand of the Night Stalker in “1984.” The second she tore down a mouthy student in her Midnight Manerobics class, we were hooked. Did she go off the rails when it was revealed she was behind some of the slashing at Camp Redwood? Sure, but to be fair, no one was innocent that season. At least she had deranged fun with it. By the end, she becomes the eternal Walmart greeter standing at the gates of the camp. Which makes sense because she’s the only one from this season we’d ever like to encounter again.
		
			
			
	Nora Montgomery (Lily Rabe)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Among the tragedies plastering the walls of the Murder House like wallpaper, few were as gut-wrenching as that of Nora Montgomery, played in her “AHS” debut by fan-favorite Rabe. Nora’s mad doctor husband Charles (Matt Ross) built her the lavish home that would become a hellish prison for so many, and her spoiled and needy attitude didn’t exactly start it off on the right foot. Rabe’s prickly characterization of Nora as a woman who craves motherhood only to push it away when it gets tough could have been unforgivable. But she still managed to make the audience care for Nora when her son was dismembered, and again when Charles decided to Frankenstein him into a monster of reanimated horror. The bewildered Nora constantly wandering the halls, unaware she is what haunts them with the melancholy of her unfulfilled life, left a stain that still lingers.
		
			
			
	Miss Evers (Mare Winningham)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	The kindly but deranged laundress tending to the soiled sheets of the Hotel Cortez is never a leading figure in Season 5, but she benefits from “Hotel”’s talent for giving its sprawling supporting cast a taste of main character energy. Devoted to mastermind serial murderer and hotel designer Mr. March (Evan Peters), Miss Evers was a tragic figure of 1920s Los Angeles who found hope in the grand vision of her maniacal boss. Winningham had single-episode appearances in “Coven,” “Freak Show” and “Cult,” but here she is central to the understanding why the Hotel Cortez is a mecca for the lost and/or depraved. Her monologue in the finale is a beautiful evolution from willfully agreeing to March’s murder-suicide evasion of justice, to her long-awaited epiphany that an eternity spent serving an ungrateful man isn’t worth the time.
		
			
			
	Beverly Hope (Adina Porter)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Is TV news reporter Beverly Hope a good character, or is Porter just that good of an actor? Regardless of the answer, no “AHS” list is complete without the Emmy-nominated powerhouse, and there’s no better role than the one she was nominated for. “Cult,” as a season of storytelling, is as uneven as it is heavy handed in its post-2016 election nightmare. Yet it’s hard to take your eyes off Porter’s rage-filled reporter who finds purpose in the murderous promises of Trumpster and aspiring cult leader Kai Anderson (Evan Peters). Porter found in Beverly a recognizable discontent and fury that both sides of the aisle wrestled with in the aftermath of 2016. Despite her blood-soaked misdeeds, Beverly became a somewhat sympathetic figure once she was confronted with the all-too-real disappointment people find in the idols they glorify, who break promises as quickly as they make them. Ultimately, Beverly was a hero for snuffing out Kai, even if she is the one who helped first inflate his ego.
		
			
			
	Agnes Mary Winstead (Kathy Bates)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	A decade later, who could have predicted “Roanoke” would be the most controversial season of the series? Still, it will always get credit for its creative structure, as a sharply rendered true-crime docuseries that switches halfway through to damn the actors of said series to their own nightmarish fates. At the switch, audiences meet Agnes Mary Winstead, a devoted thespian who has taken her role as the Mad Butcher of the Roanoke Colony too far and comes back to stalk the co-stars and crew that spurned her. Bates’ unhinged embrace of Agnes’ psychosis was genuinely thrilling. But it is also a rather pointed commentary on actors who disappear into their roles, showing the lonely spectrum of skill and sadness one can face when committing to the craft. Her execution by the cleaver of the real Mad Butcher was also pointed.
		
			
			
	Dandy Mott (Finn Wittrock)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Freak Show” was pretty clear on its stance of who you should call a freak, and that was Dandy Mott, the privileged mama’s boy whose beautiful looks masked a deep-seated evil and callous hatred for life –– human or otherwise. Wittrock’s portrayal of one of the franchise’s most vile characters is a fan favorite because Dandy was a sicko who didn’t need to be supernatural to be scary. From killing animals to robbing the world of Patti LaBelle, Dandy was a demented person with the means to explore it. Training under Twisty the Clown (John Carroll Lynch) certainly didn’t help Dandy overcome his lethal case of only child syndrome with a dash of FOMO. But he got his due in the end, proving some evils can be curbed with old-fashioned karma and Houdini’s famous Chinese Water Torture Cell tank.
		
			
			
	The Countess (Lady Gaga)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtey of FX				
					
				
	Getting Lady Gaga to succeed Jessica Lange as the grand high bitch (compliment!) of the “AHS” franchise, at least for the “Hotel” season, was an inspired choice. Giving her a character worthy of her gravitas and flare for the dramatic was a taller order. In hindsight, The Countess is more of a vibe than a character. She glided in and out of the shadows of the Hotel Cortez, feeding on Angelenos, tourists and the scenery as she made the dark souls of the hotel quake with fear. She was a living tribute to Gaga’s own prowess for fashion and fame, and proud embodiment of the misplaced fear she inspires in those who don’t understand her. The Countess was a vampire-ish villain, so it was OK that she was essentially there suck all the air out of any room she was in –– and Gaga delivered.
		
			
			
	Tate Langdon (Evan Peters)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Not a single thing Tate Langdon does in “Murder House” should be commended. Even his attempt to gently ease Violet (Taissa Farmiga) into the idea of her own death is riddled with self-serving delays. Yet, Peters is able to inspire, in his first “AHS” role, a deeply complicated empathy for the last person who deserves it. Sure, Tate had a rough upbringing with less-than-desirable parents, but murdering your classmates to work out those feelings is nothing short of reprehensible. The passing of time since “Murder House” (and America’s frustrating cycle of school shootings) has only further hindered any redemptive qualities in Tate. But the fact that audiences even tried to find some means of liking him in the first place laid the groundwork for similar ill-advised character evaluations in future seasons. Tate was a trailblazer in that way, forcing those who fell under his spell to question their own tolerance for evil.
		
			
			
	Papa Legba (Lance Reddick)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX 				
					
				
	Not everyone can be the Big Bad in the “AHS” universe. Someone has to strike fear in even the darkest hearts, and Papa Legba (the late Reddick) has a knack for it. Originally summoned in “Coven,” he has the power to grant immortality in exchange for your eternal soul. He’s the Gatekeeper of the Spirit World, a job he executes with a sinister smile. Look no further than his sick sense of humor in designing a two-for-one eternal hell for enemies Marie Laveau (Angela Bassett) and Delphine LaLaurie (Bates). Reddick’s performance infused the character with a certain ie ne sais quoi no one can replicate, but after the actor’s death in 2023, Orlando Jones stepped in for Papa’s return for “AHS13”–– and did his predecessor justice.
		
			
			
	Moira O’Hara (Frances Conroy and Alexandra Breckenridge)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy:Everett Collection / Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Murder House” set the tone for what this show could do, and one of the more memorable characters trapped on the fateful Los Angeles property was Conroy’s Moira O’Hara, the housekeeper cursed to dust its mantles for all eternity. Conroy gave Moira a quiet resolve that became a saving grace for Vivian Harmon (Connie Britton), who saw her as the old soul she was. Conversely, Breckenridge imbued Moira with a seductive allure when seen as the younger temptress by Ben Harmon (Dylan McDermott). Two sides of the same coin, Moira took the audience’s hand and gently walked us into this world, and for that, she will always be among our saints.
		
			
			
	Queenie (Gabourey Sidibe)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Try as they might, multiple seasons of “AHS” have attempted to extinguish the fire that is human voodoo doll Queenie, and none have been successful. A descendant of both the Salem witches and the New Orleans voodoo community, she walks in both worlds and is among the stronger connective threads of the franchise’s mythology having appeared in “Coven,” “Hotel,” “Apocalypse” and “AHS13.” A child of foster care, Queenie has clung to the family she found at Miss Robichaux’s Academy. Even when she questioned her place among them and felt the temptation of her voodoo roots, she found her way back to “Coven” leader Cordelia Goode (Sarah Paulson). But Queenie should be celebrated most as one of the best “AHS” scene partners. Whether it’s with her fellow witches, or tormenting the racist disembodied head of Delphine (Bates) or beating Mr. March at cards in the Hotel Cortez, she is a fiery constant in a franchise that needs it.
		
			
			
	Hypodermic Sally (Sarah Paulson)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	There is something cancerous about “Hotel,” and it is best represented by Paulson’s turn as Hypodermic Sally. As tarry and disagreeable as the drugs she injected into her veins, Sally brought a bitterness to the Cortez that could have been unpalatable. Yet, she wore viewers down to her ways as the voyeuristic jester of the hotel. She was no stranger to the pain of its story, and she often contributed to it, but there was also a lightness to her, thanks to an often side-splitting humor in her nastiness. It’s as if she found, in death, the home that eluded her in life. Plus, a fleeting scene of her cuddled up in bed lit only by the light of her phone has become a meme that embodies an entire generation of doomscollers.
		
			
			
	Elsa Mars (Jessica Lange)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Full disclosure: Fraulein Elsa Mars moved up this list after her return in “AHS13,” simply because she made the most of her one scene. Some worried the wannabe actress never got her comeuppance after “Freak Show.” But her singular appearance as a minion of Satan, resurrected at his whim to perform for a crowd that could care less, was her own form of hell –– and it is “AHS13” at its sporadic best. Charged with throwing bad women of history into the flames of hell was an amusing ritual, but her razor-sharp disdain for Margaret Thatcher (also played impeccably by Lange) was the funniest thing this show has done in years. In her original run, the Nazi Germany survivor abandoned the outcasts who trusted her to give them a safe space in a world. Lange has long said this was her passion role for the series, and she exited stage left (for a while at least) after Elsa’s swan song. What she left behind was a stunning stage presence (see: her David Bowie cover “Life on Mars”) and a special breed of bad that many characters inherited by virtue of her existence.
		
			
			
	Misty Day (Lily Rabe)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Rabe’s achingly naive swamp witch Misty Day is not unlike the fragile animals she can reanimate with her gifts. The world wasn’t kind to her delicate disposition, and yet she found acceptance and shelter among the girls of Miss Robichaux’s Academy. This sensitive soul getting one of the show’s crueler fates — trapped in hell dissecting a frog on a loop — gave “Coven” palpable stakes and grim consequences that later seasons have unfortunately undone. We want Misty safe and sound, but her loss was gutting in the most effective way. Perhaps her greatest gift is that anytime she is around, the White Witch herself, Stevie Nicks, tends to appear for an acoustic set — and that’s never a bad thing.
		
			
			
	Mr. March (Evan Peters)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Prashant Gupta / FX Networks				
					
				
	Some of Peters’ best work in all of “AHS” is done from behind the pencil-thin mustache of Mr. March, the brains and brutality behind the Hotel Cortez. This trickster god of a character who bathed in his own horrific acts of violence has become unexpectedly central to our understanding of the franchise’s mythology. In “Hotel,” he convenes the Devil’s Night serial killer dinner party, and eventually he collects souls from various corners of this universe in “AHS13.” He is among the few to enjoy his eternal damnation, spent serving as the bloody legend he always wanted to be. He’s a psychopath who revels in his own madness, and loves holding court whenever the laws of this supernatural universe allow.
		
			
			
	Myrtle Snow (Frances Conroy)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Myrtle Snow did more with a single word than most later-season “AHS” characters did with a whole storyline. The Witches Council alum turned sage advisor to Miss Robichaux’s Academy served, perhaps, the series’ best example of pure camp when she chose “Balencegia!” as her final word before burning at the stake. But she’s more than her (faux) end. From under her crimped rustic red mop, Conroy has turned a supporting character into an icon with candor and staunch loyalty for her fellow witches. These days, she exists mostly to shade those threatening the “Coven” witches and advocate for their charred end. She had to endure that fate, why shouldn’t they?
		
			
			
	Cordelia Goode (Sarah Paulson)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	Paulson’s most revisited character has become somewhat of a patron saint of the “AHS” series. Initially timid compared to her barn-burner of a mother, Fiona (Lange), Cordelia rose to become the Supreme the “Coven” witches needed. She was strong without being cruel, capable without alienating the next generation and forward-thinking for the sake of the coven. Her anguish about putting her girls through the deadly test of the Seven Wonders, and the losses she suffers along the way, has built the character into a pillar of strength in an ominous world, one that is still allowed to occasionally tremble under the pressure. Since she was one of the few to benefit from further exploration in “Apocalypse,” hopefully “AHS13” leaves Cordelia’s legacy intact.
		
			
			
	Madison Montgomery (Emma Roberts)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	“AHS” continues to retcon the story of faded-starlet-turned-bitchy-witch Madison Montgomery with repeated appearances. But initially, she was a vessel for the angst and anger that came with being a young woman unsure of how to wield her literal and metaphorical powers. Her unwavering cynicism made her eternally viral “Surprise, bitch” moment such an enduring classic, and “Coven” initially treats her as a lost cause. Then “Apocalypse” turned her into a reluctant hero, and now “AHS13” has fully bent her trajectory toward foul-mouthed savior (which culminates in lighting a cigarette off the charred corpse of Jeffrey Dahmer … because, sure). She’s best when she is at war with her fellow witches as much as herself, but her impact is undeniable. Just look at who continues to stand beside Cordelia in her various battles against dark forces. Like it or not, Madison is here to save the day.
		
			
			
	Sister Jude Martin (Jessica Lange)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	As its second installment, “Asylum” had a lot to prove to launch “AHS” into an anthology series, so it threw everything at the audience: aliens, religion, musical numbers, Nazis. But no character goes through it like Sister Jude, a ruthless nun running from a murky past who reigns over Briarcliff Asylum with an iron fist and a cabinet full of wooden whips. Her fall from grace, becoming an institutionalized shell of herself after being subjected to the very electroshock therapy she once prescribed, proved that Sister Jude reaped what she sowed. But like the best “AHS” characters, she had enough complexity that her rather sweet ending also felt justified. Jude’s reckoning with her own horrors made her the rare person you love to loathe and hate to watch leave.
		
			
			
	Delphine LaLaurie (Kathy Bates)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“AHS” can create all the creatures and demons it wants, but some of the worst threats already exist in the real world — and New Orleans nightmare Delphine LaLaurie is one of them. A murderer, enslaver, sadist and racist, “AHS” did Madame LaLaurie a service she didn’t deserve: It cast Bates to play her. Throughout her run in “Coven,” part of which was just as a disembodied head, Delphine is repeatedly and rightfully held to task for her unrepentant disregard for others. When she watches President Barack Obama on TV and bristles at being made to serve Queenie, you realize even hell isn’t hot enough for her.
		
			
			
	Lana Winters (Sarah Paulson)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	No one runs toward the screams of “AHS” quite like Lana Winters. To her credit, things couldn’t get much worse for Paulson’s intrepid journalist after she was admitted against her will to Briarcliff; subjected to electroshock and conversion therapy to reverse her queer identity; raped, imprisoned and impregnated by a serial killer named Blood Face (Zachary Quinto); and then left to kill the resulting child years later after his own killing spree. Lana’s story could have been relentlessly depressing, but instead she became an imperfect beacon of resilience. She let her ambition for fame and recognition drive her after escaping Briarcliff, but who can blame her? Later appearances in “Roanoke” and “Cult” proved she got what she always wanted: a career spent calling out injustice and evil.
		
			
			
	Marie Laveau (Angela Bassett)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	By Season 3, “AHS” needed a spark of life to shake things up, and Bassett brought it with a sizzling superiority as famous voodoo queen Marie Laveau. The series had fleeting brushes with real people before (see: the legends of The Black Dahlia and Anne Frank), but Marie was among the first to be a main character in the story. Bassett brought to this voodoo icon a banshee scream for respect as one of New Orleans’ most important historic figures. Her messy methods, killer instincts and incredibly potent threats, exquisitely conveyed by Bassett’s seething line delivery and body language, made her a force to be reckoned with, and a character who levels up this series every time she returns.
		
			
			
	Fiona Goode (Jessica Lange)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	The mean streak of Fiona Goode is something unrivaled in the “AHS” universe. A blistering presence from her first scene in “Coven,” she is a menace to anyone with a pulse, even her own kind. The fact that Fiona wasn’t a cartoonish villain is a true testament to why Lange was such a great match for the early seasons of “AHS.” Fiona was selfish, vain, scared, reckless, witty, proud and literally soulless, as revealed by Papa Legba. Lange played every one of those as if it was her defining trait. But her danger lay in the fact that she built any semblance of self on the power she was given, only to watch it slowly slip away to another. Her punishment at the end of the season was humorous, yes, but it worked because hell came for her well before Fiona was damned to it. A knotty-pine eternity with the Axman was just the cherry on top.
		
			
			
	Liz Taylor (Denis O’Hare)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Prashant Gupta / FX Networks				
					
				
	Although he had been part of “AHS” since the beginning, O’Hare wasn’t given something worthy of his depth until “Hotel” introduced audiences to the lavishly drawn Liz Taylor. Adorned in the kind of glamour and confidence that only comes from a well-earned journey of self-discovery, Liz Taylor is among the few selling points of the Cortez. The keeper of the secrets and the queen of the side eye, Liz managed to bind together the mismatched souls of the hotel. When she decides to end her life on the grounds of the Cortez instead of letting cancer take her, everyone trapped in its walls came to welcome her –– even The Countess, who was never more merciful than when she encouraged Liz to embrace her true identity. O’Hare deserves tremendous credit for the compassionate humanity he wove into Liz, and “Hotel” is better as a season and as a tourist trap because her company is among its amenities.
		
			
			
	Sister Mary Eunice (Lily Rabe)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Rabe is the most underrated ringer of “AHS” players for sheer volume of classic characters. Viewers first meet “Asylum”’s meek Sister Mary Eunice as she fumbles her way through a day as the second in command to Sister Jude. Her desperation to earn her place at Briarcliff makes her an easy target for the disembodied soul of the devil, who straightens Mary’s spine, fills her with hate and a penchant for sowing chaos. Rabe’s ability to make Innocent Mary and Possessed Mary feel like two distinct characters in one vessel is extraordinary, oscillating seamlessly between gentle soul and gleeful hellion who just wants to watch the Christians be eaten.. Mary makes other “AHS” monsters look like child’s play, and the loss of her light — even in the eyes of Nazi Dr. Arden (James Cromwell), one of those monsters — reiterated the price so many paid at Briarcliff and throughout “AHS.”
		
			
			
	Constance Langdon (Jessica Lange)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of FX				
					
				
	There is nothing the “AHS” audience hungers for more than Constance Langdon. A human horror in a series of supernatural terrors, Lange’s first (and best) role in “Murder House” remains unmatched. No wonder Murphy and company couldn’t resist anchoring “AHS13” in her resurrection as a servant of Satan with nothing better to do than help bring about the end of days for the hell of it. All she wants out of it is a misguided maternal request to be reunited with her children, Tate and Addie (Jamie Brewer), whom she repeatedly failed. But nursing the gooey corpse of the devil is hardly her worst trait. During her “Murder House” run, Constance was the acid-tongued neighborhood gossip, the negligent mother of a bad seed, the jilted wife with a gun, the jaded silver-screen wannabe who watched her dream wither on the vine, and perhaps most dangerously, the lost soul desperate for a purpose. With her Southern drawl and bigoted worldview, Constance was and remains the promise of the show’s title. For all its murderers, aliens, witches, vampires, cults, clowns, diseases, demons and carnies, she is the horror story worthy of America — a flesh-and-blood human who’d rather watch her neighbors die than be inconvenienced.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia Keeping 'Final Destination' Attraction Despite Roller Coaster Death

                          Not Pulling 'Final Destination' Fright Fest Maze
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Not Pulling 'Final Destination' Fright Fest Maze
                          ... Despite Fatal Incident
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                October 15, 2026
                
                            4:42 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 15, 2026
                                6:42 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags Over Georgia isn't pulling the plug on its "Final Destination"-themed Halloween attraction, even in the wake of the tragic death of a man on the Goliath roller coaster in Georgia ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            A spokesperson for Six Flags Over Georgia tells TMZ ... "Six Flags Magic Mountain will operate its Fright Fest programming as scheduled." We're told the maze does not contain scenes related to a theme park.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            The decision comes amid heightened attention surrounding the tragedy at Six Flags Over Georgia, where 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed Monday after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster.
      

            Authorities say he struck other riders before falling beneath the attraction, and several other guests were injured in the horrifying incident. The circumstances surrounding his death remain under investigation.
      
    
            The 'Final Destination' franchise has long tapped into people's deepest fears about seemingly harmless activities turning deadly ... famously featuring a gruesome roller coaster disaster sequence in "Final Destination 3".
      
    
            The movie's chilling premise has made the timing of Six Flags' decision particularly eyebrow-raising, with the real-life tragedy unfolding just as the park prepares to welcome guests for its Halloween festivities.
      
    
            Still, Six Flags says the maze does not feature scenes involving a theme park, despite the connection to the franchise, and the company's Fright Fest plans remain on track ... even as the real-life tragedy has left a much more sobering impression on the amusement park world.

title: Exes Katy Perry And Orlando Bloom Being Dragged Into Old Legal Battle
description:
